meta.label: VPNs
meta.attribution: Curated from public no-logs audits, ownership, jurisdiction, and open-source status - not audited by us. A VPN moves your trust from your ISP to the VPN, so trustworthiness is everything. A VPN is not anonymity (for that, see Tor). Suggest changes via Contribute.

reads.text: Compare VPNs by privacy, disclosure, openness, and jurisdiction.

axes.label: Privacy
axes.question: Does less data exposure matter more?

consumer.axes: Round 8 practical decision dials, with the S4 cost-or-values default where evidence permits.
consumer.budget: Round 8 honest budget eligibility, with S4 refusing to guess missing cost data.
consumer.archetypes: Round 8 computed answer slots matched to available category evidence.
consumer.page: Round 7 personal precedence extended in Round 9 to the shared decision page for every live category.

products.name: Mullvad
products.description: A privacy-maximalist VPN with numbered accounts, anonymous payment options, open-source apps and a flat price.

privacy.note: Mullvad's no-logging policy says it does not log traffic, DNS, connections, bandwidth, IPs or account activity.

transparency.note: Mullvad published a 2026 X41 audit of its account and payment services; reported findings did not give access to user data or weaken privacy guarantees.

openness.note: Mullvad publishes its VPN app source code publicly on GitHub.

jurisdiction.note: Mullvad is Sweden-based; jurisdiction is helpful but the stronger privacy claim comes from no-logs design and audits.

accessibility.note: Mullvad uses a simple flat monthly price and supports privacy-preserving payment options, but has no free tier.

products.name: IVPN
products.description: A privacy-first VPN with anonymous account IDs, open-source apps and a regular audit culture.

privacy.note: IVPN says its VPN servers do not store logs that can identify a customer, backed by a no-logs audit.

transparency.note: IVPN's no-logging claim was independently audited by Cure53, and annual security audits are part of its routine.

openness.note: IVPN publishes desktop app source code under its public GitHub organization.

jurisdiction.note: IVPN operates from Gibraltar, a better fit than some surveillance-heavy jurisdictions but still not a substitute for no-logs engineering.

accessibility.note: IVPN is paid and privacy-focused rather than the cheapest mainstream VPN, with Standard and Pro plans.

products.name: Proton VPN
products.description: A Swiss VPN with open-source apps, recurring no-logs audits and a reputable unlimited free tier.

privacy.note: Proton VPN publishes a no-logs policy and annual external audits of that claim.

transparency.note: Proton reports repeated independent no-logs audits, including its 2026 Securitum audit.

openness.note: Proton VPN made its apps open source and publishes independent audit information.

jurisdiction.note: Proton is Switzerland-based, giving it a relatively privacy-friendly legal posture alongside technical no-logs controls.

accessibility.note: Proton VPN offers an unlimited free tier, with paid plans for faster servers and more locations.

products.name: AzireVPN
products.description: A Sweden-origin VPN with audited no-logs claims, owned/dedicated diskless infrastructure, and a smaller mainstream footprint.

privacy.note: AzireVPN says X41 D-Sec audited its shared AzireVPN/Malwarebytes infrastructure in 2026 and found no evidence of user activity logging.

transparency.note: Malwarebytes says X41 D-Sec reviewed source code, server infrastructure and privacy architecture after Malwarebytes acquired AzireVPN.

openness.note: AzireVPN uses open protocols and published a full audit report, but its product still is not as openly source-reviewable as Mullvad or IVPN.

jurisdiction.note: AzireVPN remains Stockholm-originated, but Malwarebytes ownership means the jurisdiction story is less simple than an independent privacy-only operator.

accessibility.note: AzireVPN is a paid smaller-network service, so mainstream convenience is lower than big commercial VPNs.

products.name: AirVPN
products.description: A power-user VPN run by privacy activists, with open-source clients and less polished onboarding.

privacy.note: AirVPN states it does not monitor or log user activity and frames itself around net-neutrality and privacy activism.

transparency.note: AirVPN publishes mission, privacy and technical details, but no recurring independent no-logs audit was found.

openness.note: AirVPN's Eddie client is GPLv3 open source.

jurisdiction.note: AirVPN is Italy/EU-based, which is decent but not enough to replace independent logging verification.

accessibility.note: AirVPN is powerful and affordable, but its technical interface is less beginner-friendly than mainstream VPNs.

products.name: Self-hosted (WireGuard / Algo)
products.description: A do-it-yourself VPN that removes the commercial VPN provider, but ties traffic to your own server host.

privacy.note: Self-hosting removes a commercial VPN middleman, but your VPS/cloud host can still associate traffic with you.

transparency.note: Algo is an open-source set of scripts that lets technical users inspect and control the VPN deployment.

openness.note: WireGuard and Algo are open-source tools suitable for self-hosted VPN deployments.

jurisdiction.note: Jurisdiction depends entirely on the hosting provider and server location you choose.

accessibility.note: Self-hosting can be cheap, but it requires command-line comfort and server maintenance.

products.name: Outline
products.description: A self-hostable, open-source VPN toolkit built for censorship resistance, giving users control over the server while still requiring hosting choices and setup care.

privacy.note: Outline lets users run and control their own VPN server, reducing dependence on a commercial VPN operator while still exposing traffic to the chosen host.

transparency.note: Outline says its technology is fully open source and has been audited by Radically Open Security and Cure53.

openness.note: Outline publishes its code publicly and describes the project as open-source technology.

jurisdiction.note: Jurisdiction depends on where the user deploys the server; Outline explicitly lets users control server location and access.

accessibility.note: Outline Manager and Client simplify self-hosting, but users still need to create or trust a server and manage access keys.

products.name: Tailscale
products.description: A very usable WireGuard-based mesh VPN for connecting your own devices and servers, excellent for private access but not meant to make web browsing anonymous.

privacy.note: Tailscale says tailnet traffic is end-to-end encrypted and not inspected, while explicitly framing the product as secure connectivity rather than anonymity.

transparency.note: Tailscale publicly explains its privacy/anonymity tradeoffs and security page documents data-security, access-review and audit practices.

openness.note: Tailscale says its daemon and DERP server code are open source, while the coordination server remains closed source.

jurisdiction.note: Tailscale's privacy policy describes Canadian and US lawful-access processes, while its identity-centric design keeps jurisdiction more relevant than for no-account VPNs.

accessibility.note: Tailscale's Personal plan is free indefinitely for individuals and supports a very simple setup for device-to-device private networking.

products.name: RiseupVPN
products.description: A free, donation-supported VPN from Riseup for simple privacy and censorship-resistance needs.

privacy.note: RiseupVPN requires no account registration, reducing identity collection for casual use.

transparency.note: Riseup publishes activist-service documentation, but does not provide the recurring third-party VPN audits seen at leaders.

openness.note: RiseupVPN is based on the open-source Bitmask VPN client.

jurisdiction.note: Riseup is US-based, so legal environment is weaker than Switzerland/EU privacy choices despite its activist posture.

accessibility.note: RiseupVPN is free and no-account, but locations and capacity are limited compared with paid networks.

products.name: Mozilla VPN
products.description: A simple Mozilla-branded VPN that uses Mullvad's network and open-source client code.

privacy.note: Mozilla VPN privacy docs say the service uses Mullvad's VPN infrastructure and explains limited diagnostic data handling.

transparency.note: Mozilla publishes privacy documentation and benefits from Mullvad's network, but has less independent VPN-specific audit depth than Mullvad itself.

openness.note: Mozilla publishes the Mozilla VPN client source code on GitHub.

jurisdiction.note: Mozilla is US-based while the network runs on Mullvad infrastructure, creating a mixed jurisdiction profile.

accessibility.note: Mozilla VPN is easy to use and mid-priced, but availability is limited to supported countries.

products.name: DuckDuckGo VPN
products.description: A DuckDuckGo subscription VPN with audited no-logs claims, full-device coverage, and browser-managed setup across supported markets.

privacy.note: DuckDuckGo's subscription terms say it does not keep VPN activity logs and cannot tie VPN use to an individual.

transparency.note: DuckDuckGo published a 2025-2026 Securitum audit that validated its VPN no-logs policy and supporting infrastructure.

openness.note: DuckDuckGo VPN uses the open WireGuard protocol, but the service requires the DuckDuckGo browser and does not provide config files for other clients.

jurisdiction.note: DuckDuckGo Subscription is a US-based subscription service, with separate non-US terms for UK, EU and Canada users.

accessibility.note: DuckDuckGo says the subscription VPN works across the whole device on up to five devices, but is limited to supported regions and requires the DuckDuckGo browser.

products.name: Brave Firewall + VPN
products.description: A Brave-branded, Guardian-powered paid VPN and firewall that protects the whole device but remains tied to a proprietary browser subscription flow.

privacy.note: Brave says its VPN keeps no logs of traffic, DNS requests, connection data, IP addresses or bandwidth, and uses privacy-preserving subscription credentials.

transparency.note: Brave says the Guardian-powered VPN has undergone software and infrastructure audits by independent security firms.

openness.note: Brave VPN is a proprietary Brave/Guardian service rather than a fully open-source VPN stack.

jurisdiction.note: Brave is US-based and the service is powered by Guardian infrastructure, making jurisdiction less privacy-favorable than Swiss/EU specialist providers.

accessibility.note: Brave VPN is built into Brave, supports up to 10 devices, and costs $9.99/month or $99.99/year after a trial.

products.name: Cloudflare WARP
products.description: A very accessible encrypted DNS/tunnel app that improves casual network privacy, but is not built for VPN-style anonymity.

privacy.note: Cloudflare says WARP collects limited DNS and traffic metadata but excludes payload data, so it is a convenience/privacy tool rather than a no-logs anonymity VPN.

transparency.note: Cloudflare publishes detailed WARP privacy documentation, including what data it stores and why.

openness.note: WARP uses WireGuard-derived technology but the consumer service and apps are not a fully open-source VPN stack.

jurisdiction.note: Cloudflare is a US-based infrastructure company, so legal jurisdiction is weaker than privacy-specialist providers in stronger privacy jurisdictions.

accessibility.note: WARP is free, simple to install and widely available through Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 apps.

products.name: Tor Browser (not a VPN)
products.description: A free, open-source anonymity browser for high-risk browsing contexts, with slower speeds and stricter use discipline than a VPN.

privacy.note: Tor routes traffic through multiple encrypted relays, but Tor Project warns it only protects apps configured to use Tor and cannot guarantee perfect anonymity.

transparency.note: Tor Project documents Tor's design, safety limits and public nonprofit mission, making its privacy model unusually inspectable.

openness.note: Tor Project describes Tor as free, open-source software released under a free/open license.

jurisdiction.note: Tor is operated by a distributed volunteer relay network rather than a single commercial VPN exit provider, though users still need HTTPS and careful behavior.

accessibility.note: Tor Browser is free and cross-platform, but performance, site compatibility and operational-security demands make it less beginner-friendly than mainstream VPNs.

products.name: Orbot (Tor for apps)
products.description: A free, open-source Android VPN/proxy mode for routing apps over Tor, powerful for mobile privacy and censorship resistance but slower and more specialized than a normal VPN.

privacy.note: Guardian Project says Orbot routes app traffic through Tor, hiding traffic by bouncing it through computers around the world.

transparency.note: Guardian Project documents Orbot's Tor-based model, license, source code and limitations publicly.

openness.note: Orbot is published as free software with source code available through Guardian Project's GitHub.

jurisdiction.note: Orbot relies on the distributed Tor network rather than a single commercial VPN exit provider, though Tor-use discipline still matters.

accessibility.note: Orbot is free and app-routable on Android, but Tor's slower routing and mobile-only workflow make it less frictionless than mainstream VPNs.

products.name: Opera free browser VPN
products.description: A free browser-only VPN built into Opera, useful as a convenience layer but not a whole-device privacy replacement.

privacy.note: Opera says its free browser VPN does not log browsing activity or the originating network address, with a browser-only scope caveat.

transparency.note: Opera's 2026 safety explainer says Deloitte verified its free browser VPN does not log data and that data-logging functionality is not built into the VPN.

openness.note: Opera's browser VPN is a proprietary browser feature rather than an open-source VPN client and service.

jurisdiction.note: Opera describes itself as headquartered in Norway and governed by GDPR, a stronger privacy posture than many free VPN apps.

accessibility.note: The free VPN is built into Opera browsers with no extra account or software, but it protects only browser traffic unless users buy Opera VPN Pro.

products.name: Private Internet Access
products.description: A budget mainstream VPN with open-source apps, court-tested/audited no-logs evidence, and real US/Kape ownership context.

privacy.note: PIA says Deloitte completed a third independent ISAE 3000 review of its VPN infrastructure, including configuration, management systems and dedicated IP technology.

transparency.note: PIA publishes open-source apps, two third-party audits and quarterly legal-request counts with zero logs produced.

openness.note: PIA publishes open-source VPN apps under the pia-foss GitHub organization.

jurisdiction.note: Kape describes PIA as US-based and lists it alongside ExpressVPN and CyberGhost in its brand portfolio, so audits matter more than jurisdiction alone.

accessibility.note: PIA is relatively cheap and mainstream, with broad app support and simple consumer plans.

products.name: Windscribe
products.description: A flexible VPN with a useful free tier and good transparency material, but Canadian jurisdiction and less formal audit depth.

privacy.note: Windscribe's privacy policy describes minimal VPN session handling rather than browsing-history retention.

transparency.note: Windscribe publishes transparency reports on law-enforcement requests and data available to provide.

openness.note: Windscribe has some public code and clients, but is not as fully open-source across the stack as top open leaders.

jurisdiction.note: Canada is a Five Eyes jurisdiction, so Windscribe's score depends heavily on minimal logging rather than venue.

accessibility.note: Windscribe offers a usable free tier and flexible paid options.

products.name: TunnelBear
products.description: A simple mainstream VPN with unusually readable transparency material and recurring independent security audits.

privacy.note: TunnelBear's privacy policy says it does not collect DNS queries, IP addresses or browsing data during VPN use.

transparency.note: TunnelBear published its eighth annual Cure53 audit in November 2025 and says the 2025 audit is already completed and under review.

openness.note: TunnelBear is a proprietary VPN service rather than an open-source app/provider stack.

jurisdiction.note: Canada/US ownership context limits jurisdiction score, even though the no-logging policy lowers practical exposure.

accessibility.note: TunnelBear is beginner-friendly and has a limited free plan plus simple paid plans.

products.name: hide.me
products.description: A long-running VPN with a useful free tier and recurring no-logs audit claims, but less open-source depth than the leaders.

privacy.note: hide.me says it is a certified zero-log VPN and that recent Securitum review confirmed its no-logs policy.

transparency.note: hide.me says it undergoes regular audits and that Securitum has again confirmed its no-logs policy is strictly enforced.

openness.note: hide.me uses open VPN protocols, but the service and apps are not as openly auditable as Mullvad, IVPN or Proton.

jurisdiction.note: The score leans more on audit/no-log engineering than on a uniquely privacy-protective jurisdiction story.

accessibility.note: hide.me offers a free VPN plan and paid plans, making it easier to try than paid-only privacy VPNs.

products.name: CyberGhost
products.description: A polished mass-market VPN with repeated Deloitte no-logs assurance and low prices, balanced by closed apps and Kape portfolio ownership.

privacy.note: CyberGhost says Deloitte completed a third no-logs audit covering infrastructure and operational controls.

transparency.note: CyberGhost publishes audit summaries, though the full assurance reports remain less public than open-source-app review.

openness.note: CyberGhost is a proprietary consumer VPN, so trust relies on audits and policy disclosures rather than public app/source review.

jurisdiction.note: Kape lists CyberGhost as Romania-based while Kape itself is headquartered in London, so jurisdiction is mixed rather than purely Romanian.

accessibility.note: CyberGhost is broadly marketed, beginner-friendly and competitively priced compared with many privacy-first VPNs.

products.name: PrivadoVPN
products.description: A Swiss freemium VPN with a clear no-log pitch, useful free allowance, and less public audit depth than top-tier privacy providers.

privacy.note: PrivadoVPN says it follows a strict no-log policy and does not record or retain browsing activity or connection data.

transparency.note: Public materials center on vendor no-log statements rather than a clearly published independent no-logs audit report.

openness.note: PrivadoVPN is a proprietary VPN service without the open-source app posture of Mullvad, IVPN or Proton.

jurisdiction.note: PrivadoVPN presents itself as a Switzerland-based VPN, which is a stronger jurisdiction signal than many mass-market options.

accessibility.note: PrivadoVPN offers a free plan with 10 GB of monthly data, plus paid plans for heavier use.

products.name: VyprVPN
products.description: A veteran VPN with an early public no-logs audit, but a less recent audit story and more ordinary transparency today.

privacy.note: VyprVPN still markets audited no-log protection, but its clearest public audit record is older than annual-audit leaders.

transparency.note: VyprVPN still markets itself as an independently audited no-log VPN, but the publicly highlighted audit is not recent.

openness.note: VyprVPN is a proprietary VPN service rather than an open-source app/provider stack.

jurisdiction.note: The service's current privacy case is audit/no-log policy, not a uniquely strong or simple jurisdiction story.

accessibility.note: VyprVPN remains a mainstream paid VPN with apps for common platforms, but fewer standout ease/cost signals than budget leaders.

products.name: TorGuard
products.description: A configurable power-user VPN with strong no-logs claims and stealth options, but weaker audit/transparency evidence.

privacy.note: TorGuard states that it does not collect or log VPN or proxy data, connection logs, traffic logs or browsing activity.

transparency.note: TorGuard publishes a privacy policy and zero-logs claims, but no current independent no-logs audit was found in its public materials.

openness.note: TorGuard is a proprietary VPN provider, so its logging claims are not backed by open client/server source review.

jurisdiction.note: TorGuard's privacy case depends on no-logs policy because its legal/jurisdiction posture is not a leading privacy differentiator.

accessibility.note: TorGuard offers many protocols and stealth options, useful for power users but more complex than beginner-first VPNs.

products.name: AdGuard VPN
products.description: A freemium VPN from the AdGuard ecosystem with an open obfuscation protocol, but limited no-logs audit evidence.

privacy.note: AdGuard VPN documentation says its no-logging policy means it does not collect, store or transfer users' personal data to third parties.

transparency.note: AdGuard has opened the TrustTunnel protocol, but public no-logs audit evidence is thinner than annual-audit VPN leaders.

openness.note: TrustTunnel, the protocol powering AdGuard VPN, is published as an open-source protocol on GitHub.

jurisdiction.note: Jurisdiction is less central than the service's technical and policy claims, which still need more third-party audit depth.

accessibility.note: AdGuard VPN offers a free plan with 3 GB of monthly traffic and paid plans for unlimited use.

products.name: OVPN
products.description: A smaller Sweden-based VPN with a court-tested no-logs story, strong infrastructure claims, and less mainstream polish.

privacy.note: OVPN says it stores no activity logs and highlights a Swedish court order where requested user information could not be produced.

transparency.note: OVPN publishes security details such as disabled syslogs, server-hardening claims, and diskless-style logging prevention, but not a recent recurring audit trail.

openness.note: OVPN supports open protocols and includes open-source components, but its full consumer app/service stack is not as open as Mullvad or IVPN.

jurisdiction.note: Sweden/EU jurisdiction is acceptable, with the stronger evidence coming from the court-tested no-log posture.

accessibility.note: OVPN is paid, supports common devices, and has fair long-term pricing, but remains a smaller provider.

products.name: Malwarebytes Privacy VPN
products.description: A mainstream security-suite VPN that improved its trust case after Malwarebytes' AzireVPN acquisition and a 2026 X41 audit.

privacy.note: Malwarebytes says its VPN uses RAM-only servers and that its no-logs policy/infrastructure were independently audited.

transparency.note: Malwarebytes announced an X41 D-Sec white-box audit of the software/hardware infrastructure behind its VPN service in 2026.

openness.note: The audit improves verification, but Malwarebytes VPN is still a proprietary security-suite product rather than an open app stack.

jurisdiction.note: US corporate jurisdiction weakens the jurisdiction score despite strong technical and audit claims.

accessibility.note: Available as a standalone VPN or bundled with Malwarebytes, making it easy for existing antivirus users to adopt.

products.name: X-VPN
products.description: A widely marketed freemium VPN with a recent no-logs assessment, but lower openness and a less established privacy reputation than leaders.

privacy.note: X-VPN says a 2026 ISAE 3000 no-logs assessment found it does not collect user IPs, visited sites, DNS queries, or timestamps.

transparency.note: X-VPN publishes audit summaries and help-center details, but identifies the auditor only as a Big Four firm rather than naming it publicly.

openness.note: X-VPN remains primarily a proprietary app/service, so openness is materially lower than open-source app providers.

jurisdiction.note: X-VPN presents Singapore as its jurisdiction, which is a mixed but not uniquely privacy-leading legal posture.

accessibility.note: Freemium positioning and broad app availability make X-VPN easy to try, especially for mainstream users.

products.name: IPVanish
products.description: A mainstream US VPN with recent independent no-log audits and a real historical logging controversy under prior ownership.

privacy.note: TechRadar reported that Schellman's 2025 audit found no retained IPVanish logs, but historical logging controversy still matters for trust.

transparency.note: TechRadar reported that IPVanish launched a Trust Center with no-log audits, quarterly transparency reports, policies, and initiatives.

openness.note: IPVanish is proprietary, so its privacy case depends on audits and policy rather than open client/source review.

jurisdiction.note: Ziff Davis lists IPVanish as one of its cybersecurity brands, so US corporate jurisdiction keeps this below privacy-first non-US providers.

accessibility.note: IPVanish markets broad app support and unmetered device connections, making it easy for households to deploy.

products.name: PureVPN
products.description: A cheap mainstream VPN with current no-log audit claims, weighed down by the well-known 2017 logging trust break.

privacy.note: PureVPN's current privacy policy says it does not store browsing activity, connection logs, assigned IP records, original IPs, timestamps, or DNS queries.

transparency.note: PureVPN publishes no-log assessment materials, but the 2017 FBI/IP metadata episode remains an important caution when weighing trust.

openness.note: PureVPN is proprietary and audit/report driven, not open-source-app driven.

jurisdiction.note: PureVPN's privacy policy lists Tortola, British Virgin Islands, but jurisdiction does not erase the historical trust concern.

accessibility.note: PureVPN is low-cost, highly marketed, and offers many apps and server locations, making it easy for mainstream users.

products.name: Norton VPN
products.description: A very accessible antivirus-bundle VPN with annual no-log audit marketing, useful for mainstream users but not a privacy-first specialist.

privacy.note: Norton says its VPN has a strict no-log policy and does not track, log, or store browsing activity.

transparency.note: Norton says its no-log policy was independently re-confirmed for 2025, but report access/detail is less open than privacy-first leaders.

openness.note: Norton VPN is a proprietary security-suite product, so trust relies on Norton policy/audit claims rather than open-source review.

jurisdiction.note: Norton is part of Gen Digital's US-linked consumer security portfolio, weaker jurisdictionally than Swiss/BVI/privacy-first providers.

accessibility.note: Norton VPN is easy to buy as a standalone service or bundled with familiar Norton plans.

products.name: Bitdefender Premium VPN
products.description: A security-suite VPN that is easy for Bitdefender users, with no-traffic-log claims but fewer independent/open privacy signals.

privacy.note: Bitdefender markets Premium VPN with a strict no-traffic-logs policy, but public independent no-logs evidence is thinner than leaders.

transparency.note: The product page discloses core features and no-traffic-log marketing, but does not provide a clear recurring no-logs audit trail.

openness.note: Bitdefender VPN is proprietary and bundle-oriented rather than open source.

jurisdiction.note: Bitdefender's Romania/EU base is more privacy-favorable than many US suite VPNs, though provider trust still depends on implementation.

accessibility.note: Simple subscription pricing and integration into Bitdefender's consumer security suite make it easy to adopt.

products.name: Avast SecureLine VPN
products.description: A familiar antivirus-brand VPN with clear VPN-specific policy disclosures, but weaker trust after Avast's broader data-history baggage.

privacy.note: Avast's VPN policy says it does not log websites visited, data transferred, or IP addresses accessed, while service data rules still apply.

transparency.note: Avast publishes a dedicated VPN policy updated in 2026, but no recent independent SecureLine no-logs audit was found.

openness.note: SecureLine is a proprietary Avast/Gen product with no open app posture.

jurisdiction.note: Avast is rooted in the Czech Republic/Gen portfolio; jurisdiction is decent but brand trust is mixed by broader privacy history.

accessibility.note: Avast SecureLine is highly accessible through Avast's consumer security ecosystem and app-store channels.

products.name: HMA VPN
products.description: A long-running, very usable VPN with a 2020 no-logging reset and audit, but a reputation shaped by older logging cases.

privacy.note: HMA's current no-log page says it does not collect original IP addresses, DNS queries or online activity, though older logging cases still affect trust.

transparency.note: HMA's current privacy page says VerSprite independently reviewed its no-log posture, but the review is older than current annual-audit leaders.

openness.note: HMA is a proprietary VPN with trust based on policy and audit rather than open-source review.

jurisdiction.note: HMA's UK/Gen/Avast context and older history keep jurisdiction/trust below privacy-first providers.

accessibility.note: HMA lists apps for major desktop, mobile and Android TV platforms, plus 100+ locations and 3400+ servers on its current no-log page.

products.name: NordVPN
products.description: A polished mainstream VPN with repeated no-logs audits and strong usability, but closed apps and Nord/Surfshark group consolidation.

privacy.note: NordVPN says Deloitte Lithuania completed its sixth no-logs assurance engagement under ISAE 3000 (Revised), assessing its systems from Nov. 10-Dec. 12, 2025.

transparency.note: NordVPN says the full sixth Deloitte assurance report is available to users after logging in, which is useful but still not fully public.

openness.note: Nord publishes its Linux client source, but the broader consumer app stack remains less open than fully open-app providers.

jurisdiction.note: NordVPN's Panama positioning is favorable, but Nord Security and Surfshark finalized a merger while keeping separate infrastructure and roadmaps.

accessibility.note: NordVPN is polished, widely reviewed and accessible to mainstream users, with broad app support.

products.name: Surfshark
products.description: A low-cost mainstream VPN with unlimited devices, Deloitte no-logs assurance and mostly closed apps under the Nord/Surfshark group context.

privacy.note: Surfshark says Deloitte assured its no-logs policy in 2023 and 2025 and that it uses RAM-only servers.

transparency.note: Surfshark summarizes Deloitte no-logs assurance and RAM-only infrastructure, but detailed assurance remains less open than source review.

openness.note: Surfshark is mostly closed-source, so openness is much lower than audited open-app providers.

jurisdiction.note: Surfshark is Netherlands-based and merged with Nord Security while the brands continued with separate infrastructure and product roadmaps.

accessibility.note: Surfshark is competitively priced and supports unlimited devices, a strong ease/cost signal.

products.name: ExpressVPN
products.description: A polished premium VPN with extensive audits and RAM-only server architecture, but closed apps and Kape portfolio ownership concerns.

privacy.note: KPMG assessed ExpressVPN's TrustedServer architecture and privacy controls as of February 2025 with no identified issues on activity logging safeguards.

transparency.note: ExpressVPN says it has published 23 third-party audits to date, though users still depend on reports rather than fully source-reviewable apps.

openness.note: ExpressVPN is largely proprietary despite publishing audit material and some protocol work.

jurisdiction.note: ExpressVPN is BVI-positioned but officially joined Kape Technologies, whose current brand page lists ExpressVPN among Kape's top brands.

accessibility.note: ExpressVPN is polished and beginner-friendly, but its pricing is premium compared with budget VPNs.

products.name: Perfect Privacy
products.description: A long-running, power-user VPN with a strict no-traffic-logs policy, multi-hop tools and a relatively high price.

privacy.note: Perfect Privacy says it does not record user traffic, IP addresses, access times, duration or per-user bandwidth.

transparency.note: The privacy policy is unusually explicit about VPN data minimization, but no current public third-party no-logs report was found.

openness.note: Perfect Privacy says it uses open-source software and in-house privacy tools, but its full client stack is not source-reviewable like Mullvad or IVPN.

jurisdiction.note: The current privacy policy lists CyberDock IT Solutions GmbH in Hamburg, Germany, putting the service under EU/German privacy law.

accessibility.note: Perfect Privacy is feature-rich but priced above many mainstream VPNs and aimed more at technical users.

products.name: PrivateVPN
products.description: A Sweden-based consumer VPN with simple apps, broad device support and a stated no-logs policy, but limited public audit evidence.

privacy.note: PrivateVPN says it does not log browsing history, traffic destination, timestamps, DNS queries, IP addresses, data content or bandwidth.

transparency.note: PrivateVPN's privacy policy is clear, but no public independent no-logs audit was found during this review.

openness.note: PrivateVPN publishes consumer apps and setup guides, but does not present the service as open source.

jurisdiction.note: PrivateVPN Global AB is listed as the data controller at a Sweden address, giving it an EU/Swedish legal setting.

accessibility.note: PrivateVPN advertises simple one-click setup, 63 country locations and a 30-day money-back guarantee.

products.name: CactusVPN
products.description: A smaller VPN and Smart DNS provider with straightforward pricing and a public Securitum no-logs audit claim.

privacy.note: CactusVPN states that it does not keep logs and frames the service around privacy rather than ad monetization.

transparency.note: CactusVPN says Securitum verified its no-logs claim and highlights that audit on its pricing page.

openness.note: CactusVPN offers apps and setup support but does not present its VPN clients as open-source software.

jurisdiction.note: CactusVPN says it started as a small company in Moldova, a non-5-Eyes jurisdiction but less familiar to most users than EU/Swiss bases.

accessibility.note: CactusVPN's pricing page lists locked renewal pricing, Smart DNS included, unlimited devices and a 30-day refund window.

products.name: StrongVPN
products.description: A long-running US-based VPN with a clear zero-logging policy and mainstream ease, but limited public audit evidence.

privacy.note: StrongVPN says it is a zero-logging VPN and does not collect or log service traffic.

transparency.note: The privacy policy is detailed about service, site and third-party data, but no public independent no-logs audit was found.

openness.note: StrongVPN is a proprietary consumer VPN and does not present its apps as open source.

jurisdiction.note: StrongVPN is operated by Strong Technology LLC and stores or transfers personal data in the United States and other locations.

accessibility.note: StrongVPN is a mature mainstream service with simple plans and broad app support.

products.name: VPN Unlimited
products.description: KeepSolid's consumer VPN with broad device support and a stated no-logging policy, but a US company base and proprietary apps.

privacy.note: KeepSolid says its VPN products do not monitor, store or log online activity, metadata, DNS requests or post-session IP addresses.

transparency.note: KeepSolid's privacy policy details VPN product data collection, but no public independent no-logs audit was found.

openness.note: VPN Unlimited is a proprietary VPN product rather than an open-source, source-reviewable client stack.

jurisdiction.note: KeepSolid lists a New York, United States address in its privacy policy contact section.

accessibility.note: VPN Unlimited markets multiple protocols, wide device support and budget-friendly subscription bundles.

products.name: F-Secure VPN
products.description: A Finnish security-company VPN that is easy for suite users, but keeps temporary service logs and is less privacy-maximalist.

privacy.note: F-Secure says it does not keep logs of external VPN connections, but does process metadata and keeps temporary abuse/service logs for up to 90 days.

transparency.note: The Total privacy notice clearly separates VPN feature data, including metadata, retention and third-party-provider processing.

openness.note: F-Secure VPN is part of a proprietary security suite rather than an open-source VPN client project.

jurisdiction.note: F-Secure presents the VPN as a Finnish company service where users benefit from EU data protection and commerce laws.

accessibility.note: F-Secure VPN is packaged as a one-click privacy feature for common consumer devices.

products.name: Avira Phantom VPN
products.description: A widely distributed VPN inside Avira's consumer security stack, with a free tier and simple controls but limited independent VPN transparency.

privacy.note: Avira says Phantom VPN does not store or log customer data, while collecting setup and optional diagnostic data.

transparency.note: Avira documents what Phantom VPN stores, but no public independent VPN no-logs audit was found.

openness.note: Avira Phantom VPN is a proprietary security-suite VPN rather than a source-reviewable open-source client.

jurisdiction.note: Avira Operations GmbH is presented as part of NortonLifeLock, making the privacy picture less simple than a small independent EU VPN.

accessibility.note: Avira offers Phantom VPN across desktop and mobile platforms, including as part of its free and paid security bundles.

products.name: Hotspot Shield
products.description: A large freemium VPN with an audit page and clear VPN privacy notice, but ads and device identifiers in the free-product model.

privacy.note: Hotspot Shield's VPN notice says it does not associate browsing activity with users, but logs session duration, bandwidth, domains in aggregate and device hashes.

transparency.note: Hotspot Shield publishes a security-audit page and a product-specific VPN privacy notice.

openness.note: Hotspot Shield is a proprietary VPN; the public evidence is policy and audit material rather than app source review.

jurisdiction.note: Hotspot Shield is under Pango/Aura's US-oriented privacy framework rather than a privacy-specialist jurisdiction.

accessibility.note: Hotspot Shield is widely available, freemium and beginner-friendly across major platforms.

products.name: McAfee Secure VPN
products.description: A convenience VPN inside McAfee's broader security products, easier to adopt than to independently verify.

privacy.note: McAfee says its VPN may collect telemetry but not originating IP address, DNS queries or apps/sites used while connected.

transparency.note: McAfee's general privacy notice is extensive, but the VPN lacks the dedicated audit trail seen in stronger privacy-first VPNs.

openness.note: McAfee Secure VPN is a proprietary feature within a commercial security suite.

jurisdiction.note: McAfee identifies itself as a United States company and notes that personal information may be accessible to US authorities.

accessibility.note: McAfee Secure VPN is easy for existing McAfee users because VPN is bundled into mainstream consumer protection plans.

products.name: Astrill VPN
products.description: A pricey, censorship-circumvention-oriented VPN with proprietary obfuscation tools and some retained connection records.

privacy.note: Astrill says active-session IP data is removed after disconnection, but it keeps the last 20 connection records for support.

transparency.note: Astrill's privacy notice details retained connection records, but no current public independent no-logs audit was found.

openness.note: Astrill relies on proprietary apps and protocols rather than open-source client transparency.

jurisdiction.note: Astrill's privacy notice lists Veloxee Corp. in Vaduz, Liechtenstein.

accessibility.note: Astrill is powerful for restrictive networks but expensive and more specialist than mass-market VPNs.

products.name: Psiphon
products.description: A free, open-source censorship-circumvention tool that can be invaluable under blocking, but is not a no-logs privacy VPN.

privacy.note: Psiphon discloses collection of protocol, duration, bytes transferred, geography/ISP and limited domain/IP data for up to 90 days before aggregation.

transparency.note: Psiphon's privacy policy is unusually explicit that it is a circumvention service with operational data collection, not a no-logs VPN.

openness.note: Psiphon describes itself as open source and publishes project repositories through Psiphon Inc. on GitHub.

jurisdiction.note: Psiphon says it is a Canadian corporation with its head office in Ontario.

accessibility.note: Psiphon is free and designed for users facing censorship or blocked access, with mobile and desktop distribution paths.

products.name: Amnezia VPN
products.description: An open-source VPN app and service designed for self-hosting, obfuscation and censorship resistance, with a newer managed VPN option.

privacy.note: Amnezia says self-hosted use keeps server data local and its policy says Premium follows a strict no-logs policy.

transparency.note: Amnezia documents 2022, 2024 and 2025 7ASecurity audits, including app and server-component review.

openness.note: The Amnezia client is open-source and published on GitHub under GPL-3.0.

jurisdiction.note: Amnezia says foreign requests without proper legal basis in Romania or the EU cannot be fulfilled.

accessibility.note: Amnezia offers self-hosted, free and Premium modes, but self-hosting still requires a VPS or technical comfort.

products.name: NetBird
products.description: An open-source WireGuard-based private network for connecting your own devices, closer to Tailscale than a public exit VPN.

privacy.note: NetBird creates WireGuard-based private networks rather than selling anonymous shared exit nodes; privacy depends on self-hosting or cloud trust.

transparency.note: NetBird publishes public documentation and a public GitHub repository for its overlay network stack.

openness.note: NetBird describes itself as an open-source Zero Trust Networking platform that can be self-hosted.

jurisdiction.note: Self-hosting improves jurisdictional control, while cloud use shifts trust to NetBird's hosted control plane and terms.

accessibility.note: NetBird is simpler than raw WireGuard for homes and teams, but it is still a private-network tool rather than a one-click consumer VPN.

products.name: Netmaker
products.description: A WireGuard network-management platform for self-hosted or enterprise private networks, useful for teams but not a consumer anonymity VPN.

privacy.note: Netmaker is for building WireGuard networks between user-controlled devices and sites, so privacy depends on deployment ownership.

transparency.note: Netmaker publishes public documentation and a GitHub repository for its WireGuard network automation platform.

openness.note: The Netmaker repository describes an open-source platform for automating virtual networks with WireGuard.

jurisdiction.note: Self-hosted Netmaker can keep control-plane jurisdiction under the operator's chosen server and organization.

accessibility.note: Netmaker is powerful but expects comfort with servers, WireGuard concepts and network administration.

products.name: Headscale
products.description: A self-hosted open-source coordination server for Tailscale-style private networks, good for technical users who want more control.

privacy.note: Headscale lets self-hosters run the coordination server for a single tailnet instead of using Tailscale's hosted control plane.

transparency.note: Headscale publishes documentation and a public GitHub repository for the control-server implementation.

openness.note: Tailscale describes Headscale as an open-source alternative to the Tailscale coordination server.

jurisdiction.note: Self-hosting the control server lets the operator choose hosting jurisdiction, though exit-node traffic still depends on user configuration.

accessibility.note: Headscale is aimed at self-hosters and hobbyists, so setup burden is much higher than a managed consumer VPN.

products.name: Lantern
products.description: A nonprofit-aligned censorship-circumvention VPN with open-source clients and a focus on access in restricted networks.

privacy.note: Lantern's privacy policy describes Lantern VPN as a no-logs VPN for secure, private and uncensored access, while still collecting account/support data where needed.

transparency.note: Lantern describes itself as a 501(c)(3) nonprofit with open-source code and multiple independent audits, built for censorship-circumvention use cases.

openness.note: Lantern's GitHub repository describes an open-source VPN for speed, privacy and censorship circumvention.

jurisdiction.note: Lantern's privacy policy identifies a US-linked organization, so jurisdiction fit is weaker than services based in stronger privacy jurisdictions.

accessibility.note: Lantern is free to download on major platforms and emphasizes access in difficult censorship environments.

products.name: Calyx VPN
products.description: A free VPN from The Calyx Institute, useful for Android/CalyxOS users who need a simple nonprofit-run privacy layer.

privacy.note: F-Droid describes Calyx VPN as anonymous VPN usage with no user accounts and no logging.

transparency.note: CalyxOS documents the app as a custom branded build of the open-source LEAP Bitmask client, preconfigured for Calyx.

openness.note: Calyx VPN is based on Bitmask and distributed through F-Droid, aligning better with open-source review than closed VPN apps.

jurisdiction.note: The Calyx Institute is US-based, so jurisdiction is not as favorable as EU or Swiss privacy-first providers.

accessibility.note: Calyx VPN is free and easy on supported Android paths, but it is much less universal than mainstream cross-platform VPNs.

products.name: iCloud Private Relay
products.description: Apple's Safari-focused privacy relay is useful for iCloud+ users, but it is not a full-device VPN replacement.

privacy.note: Apple says Private Relay is designed so no single entity can match users with Safari browsing, not even Apple or the network provider.

transparency.note: Apple publishes support and privacy documentation explaining that Private Relay protects Safari browsing through iCloud+.

openness.note: Private Relay is a closed Apple service rather than source-reviewable VPN software.

jurisdiction.note: Apple's US corporate jurisdiction and iCloud account tie-in make jurisdiction fit weaker than privacy-specialist VPNs.

accessibility.note: Private Relay is easy for iCloud+ users but is limited to supported Apple/Safari traffic rather than acting as a general VPN.

products.name: Google Fi VPN
products.description: A built-in VPN for Google Fi users, convenient on mobile but still tied to Google's account and carrier ecosystem.

privacy.note: Google Fi says it does not retain online activity, but retains traffic metadata such as connection speed without IP address for 14 days.

transparency.note: Google publishes a support explainer for how the Fi VPN handles encryption, IP replacement and retained metadata.

openness.note: Google Fi VPN is a closed carrier/account service rather than open-source VPN software.

jurisdiction.note: Google Fi is US-based and account-linked, so jurisdiction fit is lower than privacy-specialist providers.

accessibility.note: The VPN is convenient for Google Fi users, but access depends on Fi/Pixel eligibility rather than open public signup.

products.name: Trust.Zone
products.description: A Seychelles-based commercial VPN with no-logs and warrant-canary claims, but thinner public audits than the strongest privacy providers.

privacy.note: Trust.Zone says its VPN servers do not store log files and signup requires only email.

transparency.note: Trust.Zone publishes privacy and warrant-canary materials, but public independent no-logs audits are less visible.

openness.note: Trust.Zone is a closed commercial VPN service, not an open-source VPN stack.

jurisdiction.note: Trust.Zone says it is located under Seychelles jurisdiction outside the 14 Eyes countries.

accessibility.note: Trust.Zone is a conventional paid VPN with free trial positioning and broad consumer device support.

products.name: VPN.ac
products.description: A Romania-based VPN that is unusually explicit about temporary connection logs, making it transparent but not a strict no-logs fit.

privacy.note: VPN.ac says it does not monitor activity but collects connection logs including IPs, times and transferred data for session troubleshooting/security.

transparency.note: VPN.ac is clear in its legal and privacy pages that connection logs are kept briefly and erased after sessions close.

openness.note: VPN.ac is a proprietary commercial VPN rather than source-reviewable VPN software.

jurisdiction.note: VPN.ac is operated from Romania, but the temporary connection-log policy lowers the jurisdiction advantage.

accessibility.note: VPN.ac is a normal paid VPN service with mainstream platform support, though it is less recognizable than larger providers.

products.name: Cryptostorm
products.description: A technical, token-based VPN with strong privacy posture and public configs, but less polish and mainstream accessibility.

privacy.note: Cryptostorm says its VPN servers never save data that can identify a customer and uses token-based network access.

transparency.note: Cryptostorm states that all server-side configs are public and describes exactly what operational logging exists.

openness.note: Cryptostorm advertises no proprietary code and public server-side configurations.

jurisdiction.note: Cryptostorm's decentralized/token model reduces account linkage, but its legal venue and operating structure are less legible than simpler providers.

accessibility.note: Cryptostorm is built for privacy enthusiasts and token users, so setup and support are less friendly than mainstream VPN apps.

products.name: Namecheap FastVPN
products.description: A cheap, easy VPN from a domain registrar, useful for basic Wi-Fi protection but weaker on public audit depth and openness.

privacy.note: Namecheap markets FastVPN with a strict no-log policy and says it will not track, collect or share logs.

transparency.note: FastVPN publishes marketing and no-log claims, but public independent audit evidence is thinner than leading audited providers.

openness.note: FastVPN is a proprietary commercial VPN, not an open-source VPN client or network.

jurisdiction.note: The strongest public claim is no-logs; jurisdiction and audit depth are not as strong a fit as privacy-first specialists.

accessibility.note: FastVPN is budget-oriented, simple to buy and offers broad consumer support through Namecheap.

products.name: Hola VPN
products.description: A specific cautionary free VPN example: its free model can make users peers in a wider proxy network.

privacy.note: Hola's privacy policy says free users may be peers on the Bright Data network and that it may collect IP address, installed apps and log data.

transparency.note: Hola discloses the peer-network tradeoff and categories of collected data, which makes the caution visible rather than hidden.

openness.note: Hola is a proprietary VPN/proxy service, not a source-reviewable open-source privacy tool.

jurisdiction.note: Hola's free plan depends on the Bright Data network model, making trust and legal exposure less straightforward than a conventional paid VPN.

accessibility.note: Hola is very easy to install and use because the free plan is funded by the peer-network model rather than a subscription.

products.name: Generic free VPN apps
products.description: The honest floor: anonymous-looking free VPN apps that may monetize attention, traffic or device data.

privacy.note: The FTC warns some VPN apps are free because they sell ads or share information with third parties.

transparency.note: A 2026 TechRadar investigation found 77% of studied Android VPNs failed basic transparency/accountability tests, including weak or inaccessible privacy policies.

openness.note: Generic free VPN apps are typically closed and opaque, giving users little way to verify logging or traffic handling.

jurisdiction.note: Opaque ownership and unclear legal venue make jurisdiction hard for users to evaluate.

accessibility.note: Free VPN apps are highly accessible, but TechRadar found the 2,666 Android VPNs with major transparency flaws still had over 2 billion combined downloads.

products.name: WireGuard
products.description: A modern open-source VPN protocol rather than a VPN provider; useful when the real choice is self-hosting or choosing providers that use auditable, simple tunneling tech.

privacy.note: WireGuard is a secure layer-3 network tunnel; logging depends on the operator rather than a built-in commercial VPN account model.

transparency.note: WireGuard is public protocol/software with a compact design that is widely reviewed and documented.

openness.note: WireGuard is free and open-source software rather than a closed VPN app.

jurisdiction.note: Because WireGuard is a protocol, legal venue depends on where and by whom the server is operated.

accessibility.note: WireGuard is supported by many apps and platforms, but manual key/routing setup is still more technical than a mainstream VPN subscription.

products.name: OpenVPN Community Edition
products.description: The long-running open-source OpenVPN stack for people who need flexible self-hosted VPN infrastructure and can manage the operational complexity.

privacy.note: OpenVPN CE is self-operated VPN software, so privacy and logging depend on the operator's server configuration.

transparency.note: OpenVPN publishes community downloads, docs, release information and a detailed OpenVPN 2.6 manual.

openness.note: OpenVPN Community Edition is described by OpenVPN as a free open-source project maintained by a global community.

jurisdiction.note: OpenVPN CE can be hosted wherever the operator chooses, so jurisdiction is controllable but not inherent.

accessibility.note: OpenVPN says Community Edition gives complete control but requires command-line and ongoing technical expertise.

products.name: SoftEther VPN
products.description: A free, open-source, multi-protocol VPN server/client project that can bridge several legacy and modern VPN protocols for technical users.

privacy.note: SoftEther is self-hosted VPN software, so privacy depends on how and where the operator runs the server.

transparency.note: SoftEther publishes project information and public source repositories.

openness.note: SoftEther says the VPN software is open source and free for personal or commercial use.

jurisdiction.note: The software can run on user-selected infrastructure, so jurisdiction depends on deployment rather than a central provider.

accessibility.note: SoftEther supports Windows, Linux, Mac, FreeBSD and Solaris and several protocols, but that flexibility is more technical than app-store VPNs.

products.name: Algo VPN
products.description: Trail of Bits' open-source scripts for setting up a personal WireGuard/IPsec VPN in common cloud providers with secure defaults.

privacy.note: Algo sets up a personal VPN controlled by the user, avoiding a shared commercial VPN provider account model.

transparency.note: The Trail of Bits repository documents the scripts and cloud-provider setup publicly.

openness.note: Algo VPN is public AGPL-licensed source code for setting up WireGuard and IPsec VPNs.

jurisdiction.note: Server jurisdiction is chosen by the user through the selected cloud provider and region.

accessibility.note: Algo simplifies deployment but still requires command-line and cloud-provider comfort.

products.name: Nebula
products.description: An open-source overlay network originally from Slack for connecting devices directly across locations without routing everything through a consumer VPN provider.

privacy.note: Nebula builds encrypted tunnels between hosts in a self-hosted overlay, so privacy depends on the operator rather than a VPN company.

transparency.note: Nebula is documented publicly and has source code available under Slack's GitHub organization.

openness.note: Nebula is described as an open-source overlay networking tool for fast, secure and scalable networks.

jurisdiction.note: Nebula's control and relay choices are deployment-specific, so jurisdiction depends on how the operator hosts its lighthouse and nodes.

accessibility.note: Nebula is powerful for technical teams, but certificate, lighthouse and routing setup make it less approachable than mainstream VPN apps.

products.name: innernet
products.description: An opinionated open-source system for managing private WireGuard networks, useful for small groups comfortable with command-line networking.

privacy.note: innernet uses WireGuard under the hood and turns IP networking into managed private network/ACL primitives.

transparency.note: The project source, issues and documentation live publicly on GitHub.

openness.note: innernet is open-source software for private WireGuard-based networks.

jurisdiction.note: The operator controls where the WireGuard peers and coordination infrastructure live.

accessibility.note: innernet is friendlier than hand-written WireGuard configs for groups, but remains a technical command-line tool.

products.name: ZeroTier
products.description: A widely used virtual-network overlay for connecting devices and networks anywhere, easier than many self-hosted meshes but more tied to a hosted control plane unless self-managed.

privacy.note: ZeroTier connects devices, clouds and networks through a software-defined overlay, but hosted management creates a service-trust layer.

transparency.note: ZeroTier publishes clients/downloads and public repositories, while commercial network management is tied to ZeroTier Central.

openness.note: ZeroTier One source is public, but commercial use and hosted-controller workflows are not as open as fully community-governed projects.

jurisdiction.note: Jurisdiction depends on hosted ZeroTier services and user deployment choices rather than a simple no-logs VPN model.

accessibility.note: ZeroTier has polished cross-platform downloads and a free starting tier, making mesh networking easier for non-specialists.

products.name: Pritunl
products.description: An open-source enterprise VPN server built around OpenVPN, WireGuard and IPsec for teams that want a managed self-hosted VPN interface.

privacy.note: Pritunl is self-hosted VPN server software, so privacy depends on the organization's server and logging configuration.

transparency.note: Pritunl publishes server docs and public source code for review.

openness.note: Pritunl describes itself as a free open-source enterprise distributed VPN server.

jurisdiction.note: The operator chooses where to deploy Pritunl servers and therefore controls the primary legal venue of traffic handling.

accessibility.note: Pritunl provides web UI and clients for OpenVPN/WireGuard, but installation and operations still require admin skill.

products.name: OpenConnect
products.description: An open-source client for connecting to many enterprise SSL VPN systems, useful when the server is imposed by work or school but the client choice can still be open.

privacy.note: OpenConnect is a client for existing enterprise VPN systems, so privacy depends mostly on the employer/school/server operator.

transparency.note: OpenConnect publishes project information and source code publicly.

openness.note: OpenConnect is an open-source multi-protocol SSL VPN client.

jurisdiction.note: Legal venue and logging are controlled by the enterprise VPN server, not the OpenConnect client.

accessibility.note: OpenConnect supports several enterprise VPN protocols, but using it usually requires technical setup and compatible server credentials.

products.name: strongSwan
products.description: An open-source IPsec/IKEv2 VPN solution for site-to-site and mobile-client deployments, strongest for technical users and organizations.

privacy.note: strongSwan is self-operated IPsec VPN software, so privacy depends on server configuration and the operator's policies.

transparency.note: strongSwan publishes documentation, release information and source code.

openness.note: strongSwan describes itself as an open-source, modular and portable IPsec-based VPN solution.

jurisdiction.note: The legal venue is controlled by deployment location and operator rather than a central consumer VPN company.

accessibility.note: strongSwan has an official Android client and broad platform support, but IPsec setup remains technical.

products.name: OpenZiti
products.description: An open-source zero-trust networking platform for making services reachable by identity and policy rather than placing users on a broad private network.

privacy.note: OpenZiti authenticates each connection with cryptographic identity, authorizes by policy and encrypts end-to-end.

transparency.note: OpenZiti publishes organization repositories, docs and Linux Foundation project information publicly.

openness.note: OpenZiti is described as a fully open-source zero-trust networking platform.

jurisdiction.note: OpenZiti can be self-operated, so jurisdiction follows the chosen deployment and controller hosting.

accessibility.note: OpenZiti is powerful and free/open, but zero-trust overlay design is more complex than a consumer VPN app.

products.name: Cloudflare Zero Trust Access
products.description: Cloudflare's managed zero-trust access route for replacing some VPN use cases with identity-aware access to specific apps and networks.

privacy.note: Cloudflare Access secures internal resources without a VPN, but traffic and policy enforcement route through Cloudflare's managed service.

transparency.note: Cloudflare publishes learning paths and implementation guidance for replacing a VPN with its ZTNA solution.

openness.note: Cloudflare Zero Trust Access is a proprietary managed service rather than an open-source VPN or self-hosted mesh.

jurisdiction.note: Cloudflare's global managed platform adds a central service provider and legal venue layer compared with self-hosting.

accessibility.note: Cloudflare provides a guided path, client software and managed tunnels for teams migrating from VPNs.

products.name: Twingate
products.description: A polished zero-trust network access service for companies moving away from broad VPN network access toward per-resource identity controls.

privacy.note: Twingate replaces network-wide VPN access with identity-based access to specific resources, but it remains a managed SaaS control plane.

transparency.note: Twingate publishes docs explaining architecture, quick starts and how it differs from VPNs.

openness.note: Twingate is a proprietary commercial ZTNA service rather than open-source/self-hostable VPN infrastructure.

jurisdiction.note: Twingate's managed service and company control plane add a provider-trust layer compared with a self-hosted VPN.

accessibility.note: Twingate markets quick deployment, app-based access and a free starting path for teams.

products.name: Teleport
products.description: An infrastructure-access platform often used instead of VPNs or bastion hosts, especially for SSH, Kubernetes, databases and internal services.

privacy.note: Teleport provides direct identity-based access to resources instead of broad network access, reducing some VPN-style trust expansion.

transparency.note: Teleport publishes public source and documentation for its infrastructure-access platform.

openness.note: Teleport has public source and self-hosted options, though many enterprise capabilities are commercial.

jurisdiction.note: Jurisdiction depends on self-hosted versus managed Teleport deployment and organization access policies.

accessibility.note: Teleport targets engineers and infrastructure teams, so it is more complex than a normal consumer VPN.

products.name: Zscaler Private Access
products.description: A major enterprise zero-trust access platform and useful contrast to privacy VPNs: strong for corporate access control, weak for individual no-logs autonomy.

privacy.note: Zscaler Private Access brokers app-specific access rather than putting users on the network, but it is designed for employer-administered access control.

transparency.note: Zscaler publishes ZTNA and ZPA product materials explaining least-privileged access and VPN replacement claims.

openness.note: Zscaler Private Access is a proprietary enterprise cloud service rather than an open-source VPN or self-hosted mesh.

jurisdiction.note: ZPA's cloud-managed architecture adds Zscaler and the employer as central trust and legal layers.

accessibility.note: ZPA is mature for enterprises but normally inaccessible to individuals outside an organization-managed deployment.
